trace.topic: The Cowan Paradox: Why AI Agents Won’t Let You Do Less Work. They’ll Make You Do More.
trace.goal: Explain the paradox that AI agents increase managerial and operational work.
expected_facts: The answer should explain that AI agents expand what teams can attempt, which often increases work.
It should argue that management, supervision, and orchestration become more important, not less.
It should connect the paradox to founder expectations about leverage.
rubric_must_haves: Names and explains the paradox clearly.
Connects the idea to day-to-day operating reality.
Includes a concrete implication for founders or managers.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should explain that AI agents create leverage, but leverage usually expands the amount of work teams attempt rather than shrinking the need for judgment and management. As a result, founders often find themselves supervising more workflows, more experiments, and more exceptions. The lesson is to expect amplified operations, not effortless simplification.
trace.prompt:
Write a blog post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: The Cowan Paradox: Why AI Agents Won’t Let You Do Less Work. They’ll Make You Do More.

Style examples from train-owned source text.
Use them for voice only. They are not evidence for claims.
Do not copy long passages verbatim.
[Style 1]
Dear SaaStr: How Can You Ensure a Smooth Transition When A New Team Member Takes Over a Customer Account?
Add value in the first interaction.  This is so rare.
There’s nothing more frustrating than getting a random email, “Hi, Tony is gone from the company. I know nothing about you, but I’m your new rep. Can we schedule a call?”
Find some way to add value.
One great way is to demo upcoming features / an upcoming release.
“Hi, I’m Jason, your next account exec. I’d love to find a way to help even more. Can I show you or anyone on your team the new AI features we’re launching shortly? There’s no additional cost for them and based on what I can see, they may radically increase your efficiency.”
Not perfect. But much better.
A second, albeit riskier, way to add value is to set up a call asking for “honest feedback on how we’re doing.”
This works, too.  Customers often just want to be heard.  The “problem” is you might have to do something about it.
[Style 2]
Dear SaaStr: When Is It Too Soon to Target Enterprise Customers in SaaS?
It too soon to target enterprise clients when you can’t support their needs 90 days
after
you close them.
It’s sort of OK in the enterprise to promise features and functionality that are sort of there … so long as you deliver them fairly promptly after the deal closes.
In fact, it happens all the time. Enterprise customers will even sign contracts agreeing to buy so long as you implement a key feature with X number of days.
But if you don’t have the team, commitment and experience to deliver that functionality at least X days after you close a Big Customer … you aren’t ready.  They’ll churn or at least, never fully deploy.
You don’t have to have the full enterprise package in the early days to close enterprise customers, especially if they have interest in you.  You’ll get some slack as a new, emerging vendor.  Especially if you have a strong deployment team.
But you have to meet your commitments and promises to them fairly soon after the deal closes.

trace.answer:
The Cowan Paradox: Why AI Agents Will Actually Pressure Us To Do More — Not Less
We’ve been told AI would make life easier, freeing us from drudgery and allowing us to focus on high-level thinking while machines handle everything else. The narrative goes like this: “AI lets you do more stuff at scale than was ever possible before.” And honestly, it does. That part isn’t wrong. But what nobody warns you about is the flip side—the one Matt Cowan calls “the paradox”: AI won’t let you take breaks anymore. Not really. The Pressure We Never Signed Up For
Matt Cowan—founder of multiple successful companies including Replit and CEO of Lovable—isn’t shy about his feelings. He’s built two companies generating hundreds of millions in revenue using AI-first development platforms. He loves it. But here’s what he said recently during our conversation at SaaStr London:
“I hate my life now because I am working harder than any human being should work.”
He wasn’t joking. He genuinely hates his life right now. And it’s not because he’s overworked—it’s because he feels like he’s drowning in the sheer volume of opportunities AI gives him access to. His teams ship tens of thousands of apps every single day. Thousands. Every day. Each app requires maintenance, updates, security patches. The list is endless. And yet, every morning, he wakes up wanting to ship more. The AI agent doesn’t sleep, so neither can he. It’s not that he’s addicted to shipping—he’s literally incapable of stopping himself. The Brutal Truth About What’s Really Happening
Here’s what most people miss: AI doesn’t free up time, it multiplies opportunity.

"20 AI Agents aren't less work than the humans they replaced.

But it's just ... easier.  They don't quit, they don't stop, they don't need promotions or even career growth.

It's easier to work with well-trained AI Agents than ... mid-pack and below humans."  More below

This is why AI will soon take 50%+ of sales jobs

Not because we don’t need sales.  But because AI can do a better job than this.

2. The Always-On Pressure
Humans naturally create boundaries. We go home, we sleep, we disconnect. AI agents don’t. This creates an insidious pressure to match their pace.
I caught myself checking AI-generated reports at 11 PM because “the agents found something important.” This isn’t sustainable, and it’s not what AI was supposed to solve.
